common_name: Black Dragon Snake Plant (Dwarf Near-Black Sansevieria)

planting.note: Pot offsets or divisions in spring into a fast-draining cactus-style mix, since this dwarf rosette is far more prone to rot than it is to light starvation.

directions: Black Dragon forms a tight, low rosette of stiff, unvariegated leaves so dark a green they read as nearly black, lacking the cream edges or stripes typical of most trifasciata selections. Its compact size keeps it well suited to desks, shelves, and dish gardens rather than the tall floor-planter habit of the species. It tolerates deep interior shade and irregular watering without complaint, but like all snake plants it needs soil to dry out fully between waterings to avoid basal rot. Give it bright indirect light if available to keep the coloring richest, though it will persist for years in much dimmer corners.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or pot divisions in spring into a loose, fast-draining houseplant mix, and keep them out of direct midday sun while new roots establish.

directions: In the wild this succulent-leaved peperomia roots into crevices on shaded rock ledges and boulder faces, forming a dense, shrubby little clump of velvety, olive-green, pale-veined leaves. Indoors it wants bright but filtered light; unlike many houseplant peperomias it can scorch in a hot south window yet also stalls out if kept in truly deep shade, so an east-facing or curtain-filtered spot suits it best. Let the growing medium dry out noticeably between waterings, since its fleshy leaves and stems store water and are quick to rot in soggy, organic-rich mixes. It stays compact and self-branching without pinching, making it an easy, low-maintenance companion for other small shade-tolerant succulents.

common_name: Fuji-No-Mine Cast Iron Plant (Cream-Streaked Deep-Shade Aspidistra)

planting.note: Divide and transplant clumps into humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade during mild spring weather, keeping newly split rhizomes evenly moist until they re-establish.

directions: Fuji-No-Mine produces broad, glossy, deep green leaves marked with a narrow, off-center creamy-yellow streak running up the blade, a subtler and more linear pattern than the heavily spotted or banded cast iron cultivars. Like the species it thrives on neglect, shrugging off deep shade, root competition, and irregular watering once established in the ground or a container. Keep it out of direct sun, which can bleach or scorch the variegated streaking, and divide congested clumps in spring only when you want to propagate or control its spread. It makes a slow but reliably tough groundcover or shaded container specimen where little else will grow.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Concolor Zebra Plant (Slender Lime-Green Speckled Haworthiopsis)

planting.note: Pot offsets in spring into a gritty, fast-draining succulent mix, and set them where they receive bright but filtered light rather than harsh direct sun.

directions: Concolor is a narrower-leaved, more slender-rosetted selection than the common banded zebra plant, with bright lime-green leaves scattered with fine white tubercles that concentrate most densely near the leaf margins rather than forming the bold horizontal bands typical of the species. It stays small and clump-forming, making it well suited to shallow dish gardens and mixed succulent bowls. Grow it in bright, indirect light; like other Haworthiopsis it is adapted to the dappled shade of rocky outcrops in habitat and can scorch in unfiltered afternoon sun. Water only once the gritty mix has dried out completely, since its fleshy leaves store moisture and rot quickly in constantly damp soil.

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets in spring and pot into gritty, fast-draining succulent mix, siting the clump in bright filtered light to preserve the cream variegation.

directions: This variegated sport overlays the dark green body and raised white tubercle bands of the common zebra plant with irregular longitudinal streaks of cream to pale yellow, giving each pointed leaf a striped, two-toned look. It stays just as compact and slow-growing as the species, offsetting over time into a tight cluster of small rosettes suited to shallow pots and succulent dishes. Bright, indirect light keeps the cream striping vivid, while deeper shade lets the leaves revert toward solid green and harsh direct sun can scorch the paler variegated tissue. Keep it dry between waterings in a mineral, fast-draining mix, since the lighter-colored leaf sections are more prone to rot than the fully chlorophyll-rich green form.
